prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(CNN) -- A Corpus Christi, Texas, hospital is investigating how up to 17 babies in a neonatal intensive care unit received overdoses of the blood thinner heparin. One of the babies died. Officials at Christus Spohn Hospital South say corrective action was taken after the discovery of the overdoses. The infant was one of 17 who may have received a more concentrated form of heparin than was prescribed, Christus Spohn Hospital South said in a statement. Heparin is an anticoagulant often used to clean the IVs of patients and prevent blood clots from forming in the lines. It came into the public spotlight last year when newborn twins of actor Dennis Quaid nearly died after receiving an overdose at a Los Angeles hospital. Nursing staff at the Corpus Christi hospital discovered the problem Sunday -- two days after the medication is believed to have been first administered, according to Bruce Holstien, president and CEO of Christus Spohn Health System. The hospital said it took corrective measures after the discovery. A preliminary investigation concluded that "the medication error occurred during the mixing process within the hospital pharmacy," Holstein said in a statement. The baby who died "was seriously ill, and we do not know at this time what role, if any, the higher than expected concentration of heparin played in this baby's death," Dr. Richard Davis, chief medical officer for the health system, said Tuesday. "Our deepest sympathy goes out to this family," he said. Twelve of the 16 other babies remain in stable condition in the neonatal intensive care unit, which cares for ill newborns. Three have been discharged, and one is critical and unstable as that baby has been since admission to the unit, Davis said. In November, Quaid's 12-day-old twins, Thomas Boone and Zoe Grace, were undergoing intravenous antibiotic treatment for a staph infection at Cedars-Sinai Medical Center in Los Angeles. According to standard procedure, nurses were supposed to clean the infants' IV lines with Hep-Lock, a drug containing a small dose of heparin, to allow the lines to flow freely. However, instead of the 10 units of heparin they were supposed to receive, the twins received 10,000 units -- 1,000 times the prescribed amount. The babies survived, apparently with no permanent injury, Quaid later told members of a House committee on government oversight, although there is no way to know whether they will show any long-term effects.

Officials at Christus Spohn Hospital South said corrective action was taken after the overdoses were discovered. The infant who died was among 17 babies who may have received a more concentrated form of heparin than prescribed, the hospital said in a statement.

The baby who died “was seriously ill, and we do not know at this time what role, if any, the higher than expected concentration of heparin played in this baby’s death,” Dr. Richard Davis, the health system’s chief medical officer, said Tuesday.

“Our deepest sympathy goes out to this family,” he said.

Of the 16 other babies, 12 remain in stable condition in the neonatal intensive care unit, which treats ill newborns. Three have been discharged, and one remains in critical and unstable condition, as the baby has been since admission to the unit, Davis said.

In November, Quaid’s 12-day-old twins, Thomas Boone and Zoe Grace, were receiving intravenous antibiotic treatment for a staph infection at Cedars-Sinai Medical Center in Los Angeles. Under standard procedure, nurses were supposed to flush the infants’ IV lines with Hep-Lock, a drug containing a small dose of heparin, to keep the lines flowing freely.

However, instead of receiving the prescribed 10 units of heparin, the twins were given 10,000 units—1,000 times the intended amount.

The babies survived, apparently without permanent injury, Quaid later told members of a House committee on government oversight. However, there is no way to know whether they will experience any long-term effects.

(CNN) — Officials at Christus Spohn Hospital South in Corpus Christi, Texas, are examining how as many as 17 newborns in the hospital’s neonatal intensive care unit may have been given excessive doses of heparin, a blood-thinning medication. One infant died.

In a statement, the hospital said the babies may have received heparin in a higher concentration than doctors had ordered. Administrators implemented corrective measures once the mistake was identified.

Heparin is an anticoagulant commonly used to flush intravenous lines and keep clots from developing inside them. The drug drew widespread attention the previous year after the newborn twins of actor Dennis Quaid nearly died from an overdose at a Los Angeles medical center.

Bruce Holstien, president and CEO of the Christus Spohn Health System, said nurses discovered the Corpus Christi error on Sunday, two days after the medication was thought to have first been administered. An initial inquiry found that the mistake happened while the drug was being prepared in the hospital pharmacy, he said.

The infant who died had already been gravely ill, according to Dr. Richard Davis, the health system’s chief medical officer. Davis said Tuesday that officials did not yet know whether the unexpectedly strong heparin concentration contributed to the death. He also expressed the health system’s deepest condolences to the child’s family.

Of the remaining 16 infants, 12 were in stable condition in the neonatal intensive care unit, which treats sick newborns. Three had left the hospital, while another remained in critical and unstable condition—the same condition that child had been in since entering the unit, Davis said.

In November, Quaid’s 12-day-old twins, Thomas Boone and Zoe Grace, were receiving antibiotics intravenously at Cedars-Sinai Medical Center in Los Angeles for a staph infection. Under normal protocol, nurses were to flush their IV lines with Hep-Lock, which contains a small quantity of heparin, so the lines would remain open.

Instead of the prescribed 10 units, however, each twin was given 10,000 units—1,000 times the intended amount. Both survived and appeared to have suffered no lasting harm, Quaid later told a House government oversight committee, though he said it was impossible to determine whether long-term effects might eventually emerge.

According to the hospital’s preliminary inquiry, the problem appears to have originated in the hospital pharmacy, where the heparin solution was mixed at an incorrect concentration before being sent to the neonatal intensive care unit. Hospital officials said corrective measures were taken after the error was discovered, including reviewing pharmacy procedures and safeguards intended to prevent similar mistakes.

One infant who may have received the concentrated medication died. However, hospital officials said it had not been determined whether heparin contributed to the death, and the case remained under medical review. Most of the other affected babies were reported to be stable, and some had already been discharged.

Heparin can be lifesaving when administered at the proper dose, but excessive amounts can cause severe or uncontrolled bleeding, a particular danger for premature and critically ill newborns. The incident underscores how a single error in preparing or labeling medication can affect multiple patients and why hospitals rely on careful calculations, independent checks and standardized pharmacy protocols.

The hospital said it would continue examining how the mistake occurred, monitor the infants who may have been exposed and make additional changes as needed. The episode also highlights the potentially deadly consequences of medication-preparation errors and the importance of rapidly identifying, reporting and correcting them.

counterfactuals.prompt: Summarize the Texas neonatal heparin overdose incident in detail, including hospital officials’ statements, the suspected pharmacy mixing error, and relevant background on the Cedars-Sinai case.
counterfactuals.output:
### Texas neonatal heparin overdose

In July 2008, 17 babies in the neonatal intensive-care unit at **Christus Spohn Hospital South in Corpus Christi, Texas**, received heparin solutions that were far more concentrated than prescribed. Heparin was being used in very small “flush” doses to keep intravenous lines from clotting, not as full anticoagulant therapy.

Hospital officials said an internal investigation traced the problem to the **hospital pharmacy**, where a batch of heparin solution had apparently been mixed at roughly **100 times the intended concentration**. The compounded solution was then sent to the neonatal unit and administered before staff recognized the error.

Two premature infants died during the episode. Hospital leaders emphasized that both babies had serious underlying medical problems and said it had not yet been established that the heparin error caused or contributed to their deaths. The other affected infants were monitored and treated as necessary; most were reported to have stabilized or recovered.

### Hospital officials’ response

Hospital president and chief executive **Bruce Holstien** publicly apologized to the families and described the event as a grave and preventable medication error. Officials said the hospital:

- Stopped using the implicated heparin preparation as soon as the problem was identified.
- Tested and closely monitored the affected infants for excessive anticoagulation and bleeding.
- Notified parents, regulators, and other appropriate authorities.
- Began an internal review of pharmacy compounding, checking, labeling, and distribution procedures.
- Removed or reassigned personnel associated with the preparation while the investigation proceeded.

Hospital physicians explained that heparin overdoses can produce severe bleeding because the drug interferes with clot formation. They also cautioned against assuming that every complication or death among the extremely premature infants was caused by the overdose. State health officials and other investigators reviewed the incident, including the pharmacy’s preparation and verification process.

### Suspected pharmacy mixing error

The Texas event was reported as a **compounding or dilution mistake**, rather than simply a nurse selecting the wrong commercially packaged vial at the bedside. The hospital’s preliminary findings indicated that pharmacy personnel prepared a solution containing about 100 times the ordered amount of heparin and that the error was not caught during the checking process before the solution reached the NICU.

That distinction was important because it pointed to several potential system failures:

- Incorrect calculation or dilution during compounding.
- Failure of the required independent double-check.
- Inadequate labeling of the finished solution.
- Lack of a final concentration check before distribution.
- Insufficient safeguards for high-alert drugs used in neonates.

Contemporary accounts varied slightly in how they expressed the intended and actual concentrations, but hospital officials consistently characterized the preparation as approximately a **hundredfold overdose**.

### Background: the Cedars-Sinai case

The Texas incident drew immediate comparisons with a highly publicized heparin overdose at **Cedars-Sinai Medical Center in Los Angeles in November 2007**. In that case, three infants—including actor **Dennis Quaid’s newborn twins, Thomas Boone and Zoe Grace**—received approximately **1,000 times the intended dose**.

The Cedars-Sinai error involved commercially packaged heparin vials of drastically different strengths. Staff intended to use a low-concentration product, commonly described as a **10-units-per-milliliter heparin lock flush**, but instead used vials containing **10,000 units per milliliter**. The vials’ similar appearance and labeling were cited as contributing factors, although investigators also identified failures in hospital storage, medication selection, and checking procedures. The Quaid twins suffered bleeding and abnormal clotting tests but survived.

Cedars-Sinai later acknowledged medication-handling failures, implemented additional safeguards, and was disciplined by California regulators. The Quaid family pursued legal claims, including allegations that manufacturer **Baxter Healthcare** had not adequately distinguished the vial strengths; they also reached a settlement with the hospital.

Thus, both incidents involved heparin—a particularly dangerous drug in newborns—but the immediate mechanisms differed:

- **Cedars-Sinai:** selection of the wrong commercially manufactured vial, resulting in an approximately 1,000-fold overdose.
- **Christus Spohn in Texas:** an apparent pharmacy compounding or dilution error, resulting in an approximately 100-fold concentration error.

Both cases became prominent examples of the need for standardized concentrations, physically separated storage, distinctive labeling, barcode verification, and mandatory independent double-checks for high-alert medications in neonatal units.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

**CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas —** One infant has died and 16 others are being monitored after a hospital pharmacy error may have exposed 17 newborns to excessive doses of the blood thinner heparin, hospital officials said.

The infants were being treated in the neonatal intensive care unit at Christus Spohn Hospital South when staff discovered that a heparin solution had been prepared at a higher concentration than intended. Officials said the error originated in the hospital pharmacy and an investigation is underway to determine how much medication each child received.

The hospital has not established that the overdose caused the infant’s death. Officials said the child had serious medical problems, and the cause of death remains under investigation.

Heparin is commonly used in very small amounts to prevent intravenous lines from clotting. Excessive doses can cause uncontrolled bleeding and other life-threatening complications.

The incident recalls the 2007 medication error involving actor Dennis Quaid’s newborn twins at Cedars-Sinai Medical Center in Los Angeles. The twins received heparin at roughly 1,000 times the intended concentration after high-dose and low-dose vials were confused. Both children survived.

Christus Spohn said it has notified the affected families, stopped using the improperly prepared solution and begun reviewing pharmacy and medication-safety procedures. State health authorities are also expected to examine the incident.

*This is a developing story and will be updated as more information becomes available.*
